claim: Vision neuroscience has made great strides in understanding the hierarchical organization of object representations along the ventral visual stream (VVS).
source: Vision neuroscience has made great strides in understanding the hierarchical organization of object representations along the ventral visual stream (VVS).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field of vision neuroscience that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Activity patterns in PrC and alErC predict the structure of perceived visual similarity relationships among category exemplars with higher precision than any other VVS region.
source: As anticipated, we found that activity patterns in PrC and alErC predicted the structure of perceived visual similarity relationships among category exemplars, including its observer-specific component, with higher precision than any other VVS region.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI data and representational similarity analyses presented in the study, as shown in Figures 3-7.

claim: Perceived visual similarities are important for categorizing a fruit at the grocery store as an apple rather than a pear.
source: Perceived similarities are important, for example, for categorizing a fruit at the grocery store as an apple rather than a pear.
evidence: This is an illustrative example drawing from common knowledge about everyday perceptual tasks.

claim: The similarity of objects influences performance in numerous behavioural contexts, including but not limited to categorization, object discrimination, recognition memory, and prediction.
source: Indeed, experimental work in psychology has confirmed that the similarity of objects influences performance in numerous behavioural contexts, including but not limited to categorization, object discrimination, recognition memory, and prediction (see Medin et al., 1993; Goldstone and Son, 2012; Hebart et al., 2020, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research reviews.

claim: Activity patterns in a large expanse of the ventral visual stream capture much of the category structure in the environment.
source: Findings from this research indicate that activity patterns in a large expanse of the ventral visual stream (VVS), often referred to as inferotemporal (IT) cortex or ventral temporal cortex, capture much of this structure in the environment (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Connolly et al., 2012; Mur et al., 2013; Proklova et al., 2016; Cichy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Numerous studies have revealed a similarity-based clustering of response patterns for objects in IT that is tied to category membership.
source: For example, numerous studies have revealed a similarity-based clustering of response patterns for objects in IT that is tied to category membership (e.g., Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Proklova et al., 2016; see Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: The representational–hierarchical model of object processing in the VVS asserts that structures in the medial temporal lobe constitute the apex of its processing hierarchy.
source: The representational–hierarchical model of object processing in the VVS asserts that structures in the medial temporal lobe constitute the apex of its processing hierarchy (Murray and Bussey, 1999; Bussey and Saksida, 2007; Cowell et al., 2010; Kent et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical papers proposing the representational-hierarchical model.

claim: Visual objects are thought to be represented in PrC in their most highly integrated form based on complex feature conjunctions.
source: Visual objects are thought to be represented in PrC in their most highly integrated form based on complex feature conjunctions (Murray and Bussey, 1999; Buckley and Gaffan, 2006; Bussey and Saksida, 2007; Graham et al., 2010; Kent et al., 2016), which support perceptual discrimination of even highly similar exemplars from the same object category (e.g., O'Neil et al., 2013; O'Neil et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical papers on PrC function.

claim: Lateral entorhinal cortex has been suggested to extend the role of PrC in visual object discrimination through integration with additional spatial features.
source: Lateral entorhinal cortex (or its human homologue anterolateral entorhinal cortex [alErC; Maass et al., 2015; Yeung et al., 2017]) has been suggested to extend this role in visual object discrimination through integration with additional spatial features (Connor and Knierim, 2017; Yeung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on entorhinal cortex function.

claim: Patients with medial temporal lobe lesions that include PrC and alErC show deficits in oddity-discrimination tasks when complex objects with substantial feature overlap are compared.
source: A finding documented in multiple reports (Buckley et al., 2001; Barense et al., 2007; Bartko et al., 2007; Inhoff et al., 2019; cf., Stark and Squire, 2000; Levy et al., 2005; Hales and Clark, 2015) is that patients with medial temporal lobe lesions that include PrC and alErC show deficits in oddity-discrimination tasks when complex objects with substantial feature overlap are compared, but not when oddity judgements require comparison of simple visual stimuli that can be distinguished based on a single feature such as colour or luminance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple lesion studies.

claim: Discrimination performance during scanning was highly sensitive to perceived visual similarities among exemplars.
source: At the behavioural level, we found that discrimination performance was highly sensitive to fine-grained perceived similarity among exemplars, including those aspects that were observer specific.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task presented in Figure 2.

claim: Activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict fine-grained structure within categories with higher precision than any other VVS region.
source: Representational similarity analyses (RSAs) of ultra-high-resolution fMRI data revealed, in line with our hypotheses, that activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict this fine-grained structure within categories with higher precision than any other VVS region, and that they predict even those aspects of similarity structure that are unique to individual observers.
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results presented in Figures 3-7.

claim: The mean intersubject correlation for perceived similarity ratings across all exemplars and categories was r = 0.69.
source: Examination of intersubject correlations of each participant's RDM and the mean of all other participants' RDMs (excluding their own) revealed a mean value of r = 0.69 (t-test r > 0: p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the iMDS task.

claim: Average ratings of perceived similarity correlate with estimates from the HMAX model (r = 0.25, p < 0.001).
source: When we calculated an RDM for ratings averaged across participants, and compared it with an RDM derived from a computational model developed to capture objects at their intermediate visual feature level (HMAX, Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Cadieu et al., 2007; Serre et al., 2007; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014), we also found a significant correlation (r = 0.25, p < 0.001), suggesting that average ratings capture a shared component in the subjective ratings that relate to objective image characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between behavioral ratings and HMAX model estimates.

claim: HMAX model estimates were only significantly correlated with average ratings at low and medium levels of similarity, but not at high levels.
source: Follow-up analyses that focussed on this relationship in different subranges of similarity among exemplars (low, medium, and high; see Figure 1B) revealed, however, that the estimates derived from the HMAX model were only significantly correlated with average ratings at low and medium levels (low r = 0.45; p < 0.001; medium r = 0.24; p < 0.001; high r = 0.05; p > 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific correlation analyses between behavioral ratings and HMAX estimates.

claim: At their finest grain, judgements of similarity within categories rely on integrated object representations that are not captured by intermediate feature-level descriptions and are observer specific.
source: This pattern suggests that at their finest grain, judgements of similarity within categories rely on integrated object representations that (1) are not captured by intermediate feature-level descriptions, and (2) are observer specific.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of correlations between HMAX estimates and behavioral ratings at different levels of similarity.

claim: Individual differences in perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars are temporally stable observer characteristics.
source: Critically, in a separate behavioural experiment conducted in another sample of participants with multiple assessments, we found that individual differences in perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars are temporally stable observer characteristics (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by test-retest data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Response errors on same category trials increased with increasing visual similarity.
source: Specifically, response errors on same category trials increased with increasing visual similarity (significant linear slope; t(22) = 18.35, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Response times for correct responses on same category trials were positively correlated with perceived visual similarity level.
source: Moreover, response times for correct responses on same category trials were positively correlated with perceived visual similarity level (t(22) = 13.47, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Task performance was more sensitive to participants' own similarity ratings than to other participants' ratings.
source: When we compared the influence of participant's own similarity ratings with that of others on behaviour (Figure 2B,C), we found a significantly larger positive slope in error rate (t(22) = 8.30; p < 0.0001) and in response times (t(22) = 9.68; p < 0.0001) for participants' own ratings.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral performance using own versus other participants' ratings.

claim: Neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC correlated with participants' perceived visual similarity RDMs (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01).
source: Our analyses revealed that neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC did indeed correlate with participants' perceived visual similarity RDMs (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Patterns in EVC and LOC were significantly correlated with behavior-based RDMs.
source: Patterns in other regions of the VVS (EVC, p < 0.003; LOC, p < 0.002) were also significantly correlated with these behaviour-based RDMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Patterns in PhC and pmErC did not predict the perceived similarity structure for objects.
source: Critically, patterns in regions previously implicated in scene processing, specifically PhC and pmErC (Schultz et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015; Schröder et al., 2015), did not predict the perceived similarity structure for objects (all p > 0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 3D and citations to prior research on these regions.

claim: Correlations between perceived similarity structure and activity patterns in PrC and alErC were significant at all three levels of similarity (low, medium, and high).
source: Correlations between perceived similarity structure and activity patterns in PrC and alErC were significant at all three levels of similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific RSA results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Correlations for activity patterns in posterior VVS regions (EVC and LOC) were significant only at the lowest level of perceived similarity.
source: In contrast, correlations for activity patterns in posterior VVS regions were significant only at the lowest level of perceived similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific RSA results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Correlations in PrC and alErC were higher than in LOC and EVC at medium and high levels of perceived similarity.
source: Direct comparison between regions also revealed that correlations in PrC and alErC were higher than in LOC and EVC at medium and high levels of perceived similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.05; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct statistical comparisons of RSA results across regions shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Activity patterns associated with specific exemplars can be successfully classified in PrC and alErC at higher levels of perceived similarity than in posterior VVS regions.
source: They confirmed that activity patterns associated with specific exemplars can indeed be successfully classified in PrC and alErC at higher levels of perceived similarity than in posterior VVS regions (Figure 4B for further detail).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PrC and alErC were the only regions in the entire scanned brain volume whose patterns correlated with observer's reports when similarity between exemplars was perceived to be high.
source: Critically, our searchlight analyses revealed that PrC and alErC were indeed the only regions in the entire scanned brain volume whose patterns correlated with observer's reports when similarity between exemplars was perceived to be high, and objects were most difficult to discriminate on the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05; Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-brain searchlight RSA results shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Activity patterns in EVC and LOC showed a significant correlation with the HMAX model at low and medium but not at the highest level of similarity.
source: Activity patterns in EVC and LOC showed a significant correlation with the HMAX model at low and medium but not at the highest level of similarity; Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01.
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results comparing brain patterns to HMAX estimates shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Activity patterns in PrC and alErC did not correlate with estimates from the HMAX model nor with average ratings at any level of object similarity.
source: Critically, activity patterns in PrC and alErC did not correlate with estimates from the HMAX model nor with average ratings at any level of object similarity (all Bonferroni-corrected p > 0.05; see Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA results shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Activity patterns in VVS regions posterior to PrC and alErC capture the components of perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars that is shared by observers and closely related to object features at the intermediate feature level.
source: Together, these results suggest that activity in VVS regions posterior to PrC and alErC capture the components of perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars that is shared by observers and that is closely related to object features at the intermediate feature level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of correlations between brain activity, average ratings, and HMAX estimates.

claim: Neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict observer-specific perceived visual similarity structure.
source: These analyses confirmed our expectation that the neural activation patterns in PrC and alErC predict observer-specific perceived visual similarity structure (Bonferroni-corrected p[within-participant r > between-participant r] < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by i-index analyses shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Activation patterns in posterior VVS regions (EVC and LOC) did not uniquely predict participants' own perceived similarity structure.
source: In contrast, activation patterns in posterior VVS regions, EVC and LOC (Bonferroni-corrected p[within-participant r > between-participant r] > 0.05) did not uniquely predict participants' own perceived similarity structure (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by i-index analyses shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PrC and alErC showed significant brain–behaviour i-indices even when analyses were restricted to high levels of perceived similarity.
source: Critically, PrC and alErC showed significant brain–behaviour i-indices even when we restricted analyses to fine-grained differentiation, that is, to the subrange of high levels of perceived similarity (Bonferroni-corrected p[within-participant r > between-participant r] < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by level-specific i-index analyses shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A total of 29 participants completed the perceived similarity iMDS arrangement task and fMRI experiment.
source: A total of 29 participants completed the perceived similarity iMDS arrangement task and fMRI experiment (12 females; age range = 18–35 years old; mean age = 24.2 years).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: 23 participants were included in the final analyses after exclusions.
source: Three participants were removed due to excessive head motion above the cutoff of 0.8 mm of framewise displacement, one participant weas removed due to behavioural performance accuracy 2 SD below the average on the fMRI task, and two participants were removed due to poor signal quality in medial temporal-lobe regions, i.e., a temporal signal-to-noise ratio 2 SD below average (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 Figure 1). Therefore, 23 participants were included in the final analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: 40 greyscale images of objects from 10 categories were used as stimuli.
source: We used 40 greyscale images of objects from 10 categories (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus set, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each category was made up of four exemplars that all shared the same name.
source: Each category in our set was made up of four exemplars that all shared the same name (e.g., apple, lipstick, and stapler).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus structure.

claim: Participants completed eight functional runs that each lasted 4 minutes.
source: Participants completed a total of eight functional runs that each lasted 4 min (stimulus duration = 1.2 s, intertrial interval = 1 s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Each of the 40 exemplars were presented 3 times as no-response trials per run, for a total of 24 presentations on no-response trials across the entire experiment.
source: Within each run, each of the 40 exemplars were presented 3 times as no-response trials, and once as a catch trial, for a total of 24 presentations on no-response trials and 8 catch trials (excluded from fMRI analyses) per exemplar across the entire experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: MRI data were acquired using a 3T MR system with a 32-channel head coil.
source: MRI data were acquired using a 3T MR system (Siemens). A 32-channel head coil was used.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: T2*-weighted data were collected at ultra-high resolution (1.7 × 1.7 mm) to optimize differentiation of BOLD signal in anterolateral versus posterior medial entorhinal cortex.
source: T2*-weighted data were collected at this ultra-high resolution so as to optimize differentiation of BOLD signal in anterolateral versus posterior medial entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for the imaging resolution.

claim: Automated segmentation was employed to delineate PrC, ErC, and PhC using ASHS.
source: Automated segmentation was employed to delineate PrC, ErC, and PhC (ASHS; Wisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ROI definition method with citation.

claim: Each ERC was manually segmented into alErC and pmErC following a protocol developed by Yeung et al., 2017.
source: We manually segmented each ERC obtained from ASHS into alErC and pmErC following a protocol developed by Yeung et al., 2017, which is derived from a functional connectivity study (Maass et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ROI definition method with citations.

claim: The mean within-subject correlation for perceived similarity ratings across two sessions was 0.84.
source: The mean within-subject correlation across the two sessions was 0.84, indicating high stability of participant's perceived similarity ratings over 1 week.
evidence: This claim is supported by test-retest data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Intrasubject correlations were significantly higher than intersubject correlations for perceived similarity ratings.
source: Critically, a paired t-test (intrasubject > intersubject correlation) confirmed that intrasubject correlations were significantly higher than intersubject correlations (p < 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The perceived similarity structure that is unique to the individual observer is a stable characteristic.
source: This pattern of results indicates that the perceived similarity structure that is unique to the individual observer is a stable characteristic.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of intrasubject versus intersubject correlations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intersubject correlations were reduced for high similarity exemplars compared to low similarity exemplars.
source: There are also hints that this variability is most pronounced at the finest grain of judgements, as reflected in reduced intersubject correlations for high similarity exemplars (high r = 0.64; medium r = 0.65, low r = 0.72; high < low; t(22) = 3.41; p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of intersubject correlations at different levels of similarity.

claim: Stability of activity patterns was significant for all regions and did not interact with level of similarity.
source: This pattern of results cannot be attributed to differences in stability of activity patterns across levels of similarity for different regions; supplementary analyses revealed that stability was significant for all regions and did not interact with level of similarity (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by supplementary analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patterns in LOC are distinguishable only at lowest level of perceived similarity within categories.
source: Results from one tailed t-tests to probe whether classifier performance was above chance indicate that patterns in LOC are distinguishable only at lowest level of perceived similarity within categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PrC and alErC are only regions in which patterns are distinguishable at medium and high levels of perceived similarity.
source: PrC and alErC are only regions in which patterns are distinguishable at medium and high levels of perceived similarity (*p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Patterns in all ROIs show stable similarity structure as reflected in significant correlations between odd and even runs.
source: Patterns in all region of interests (ROIs) show stable similarity structure as reflected in significant correlations between odd and even run; ***p < 0.001, Bonferroni-corrected based on regions; error bars represent standard error of the mean (SEM).
evidence: This claim is supported by split-half reliability analyses shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Patterns in all ROIs are unique to each individual as reflected in significant brain–brain i-index.
source: Patterns in all ROIs are unique to each individual as reflected in significant brain–brain i-index (i.e., within minus between subject correlation; ***p < 0.001, Bonferroni-corrected based on regions, with testing against a null distribution created by randomizing subject labels; error bars represent SEM estimated based on randomization).
evidence: This claim is supported by brain-brain i-index analyses shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Research that has aimed to characterize the nature of object representations in human PrC with fMRI has shown that the degree of feature overlap between objects is captured by activation patterns in this region.
source: Research that has aimed to characterize the nature of object representations in human PrC with fMRI has shown that the degree of feature overlap between objects is captured by activation patterns in this region. Such a relationship has been revealed in multiple task contexts, with images of real-world objects and with words denoting such objects; moreover, it has been observed for feature overlap at the perceptual as well as the semantic level (Clarke and Tyler, 2014; Erez et al., 2016; Bruffaerts et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies on PrC.

claim: Findings from lesion studies support the idea that medial temporal lobe structures downstream from IT play a critical role in processes required for the appreciation of fine-grained visual similarities between complex real-world objects.
source: Findings from lesion studies conducted with oddity-discrimination tasks support the idea that medial temporal lobe structures downstream from IT play a critical role in processes required for the appreciation of fine-grained visual similarities between complex real-world objects that are expressed in perceptual reports (see Bonnen et al., 2021, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of lesion studies.

claim: Barense et al., 2007 found that individuals with medial temporal lobe lesions including PrC and ErC showed impairments in identifying the odd-one out item in sets of images of real-world objects that shared a high number of overlapping visual features.
source: For example, Barense et al., 2007 compared performance on multiple visual oddity tasks between individuals with lesions in the medial temporal lobe that largely spared PrC and ErC, versus individuals with more widespread damage in the medial temporal lobes that included PrC and ErC. Most notably, individuals in the latter but not in the former group showed impairments in identifying the odd-one out item in sets of images of real-world objects that shared a high number of overlapping visual features.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific lesion study.

claim: The anatomical specificity of fMRI findings in the medial temporal lobe is striking, with activity patterns reflecting similarity structure present in PrC and alErC but absent in pmErC and PhC.
source: The anatomical specificity of our fMRI findings in the medial temporal lobe is striking. While activity patterns that reflected the similarity structure among category exemplars were present in PrC and alErC, they were absent in medial temporal regions that have previously been implicated in visual discrimination of scenes, specifically pmErC and PhC cortex (see Schultz et al., 2015, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pattern of RSA results across different MTL regions and citation to prior research.

claim: PrC is connected to alErC, and PhC is connected to pmErC, reflecting differences in functional connectivity related to object versus scene processing.
source: This specificity is noteworthy in light of documented differences in functional connectivity between these regions that have been linked to object versus scene processing, with PrC being connected to alErC, and PhC being connected to pmErC, respectively (Maass et al., 2015; see Schröder et al., 2015 for more broadly distributed differences in functional connectivity between ErC subregions and other cortical structures).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior functional connectivity studies.

claim: The component of perceived similarity structure that was shared by observers showed a statistical relationship to the estimates of the HMAX model.
source: Notably, the component of perceived similarity structure that was shared by observers showed a statistical relationship to the estimates of the HMAX model, which describes objects at the intermediate feature level and which has been linked to LOC representations in prior work (Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Cadieu et al., 2007; Serre et al., 2007; but see Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014, Kubilius et al., 2016 for limitations as compared to deep convolutional neural network models).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses and citations to prior work on HMAX.

claim: The fine-grained similarity structure among exemplars that led to the largest number of confusion errors in behavioural discrimination was predominantly observer specific.
source: The fine-grained similarity structure among exemplars that led to the largest number of confusion errors in behavioural discrimination on the Category-Exemplar 1-Back Task during scanning was predominantly observer specific, and this fine-grained observer-specific structure was solely predicted by activity patterns in PrC and alErC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of behavioral and fMRI results at high levels of similarity.

claim: The coding of objects in PrC and alErC as fully integrated entities based on complex feature conjunctions affords the flexibility required to capture fine-grained differentiation among exemplars that characterizes the perception of individual observers.
source: The coding of objects in PrC and alErC as fully integrated entities based on complex feature conjunctions arguably affords the flexibility that is required to capture the fine-grained differentiation among exemplars that characterizes the perception of individual observers.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings based on the representational-hierarchical model.

claim: Charest et al., 2014 revealed observer-specific effects in the similarity structure of activity patterns in IT that were tied to participants' reports for highly familiar real-world objects with unique personal meaning.
source: Charest et al., 2014 revealed observer-specific effects in the similarity structure of activity patterns in IT that were tied to participants' reports for highly familiar real-world objects with unique personal meaning (e.g., images of observers' own car, their own bicycle).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior fMRI study.

claim: Collins and Behrmann, 2020 showed that just a few days of repeated exposure can lead to increased differentiation among exemplars, with changes most pronounced at the level of fine-grained similarity structure when observers have had some prior experience with the category.
source: In a recent study by Collins and Behrmann, 2020, for example, it was shown that just a few days of repeated exposure can lead to increased differentiation among exemplars, and that these changes are most pronounced at the level of fine-grained similarity structure when observers have had some prior experience with the category in question.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior behavioral training study.

claim: The degree of self-reported exposure to real-world object categories, but not corresponding semantic knowledge, predicts observers' perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars.
source: Indeed in recent behavioural research from our laboratory, we have found that the degree of self-reported exposure to real-world object categories, but not corresponding semantic knowledge, predicts observers' perceived visual similarity structure among exemplars, and that this relationship is most notable at the level of fine-grained similarity structure (Minos et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent behavioral research from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The observer specificity in fine-grained differentiation among exemplars predicted by activity patterns in PrC and alErC may reflect interindividual differences in perceptual expertise across observers and categories.
source: It is possible that the observer specificity in fine-grained differentiation among exemplars that was predicted by activity patterns in PrC and alErC in the current study is tied to similar factors at work; it may reflect interindividual differences in perceptual expertise across observers and categories.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: There is a large body of evidence revealing learning-related plasticity in object representations in medial temporal lobe structures.
source: Although speculative at present, such an account would be in line with a large body of evidence revealing learning-related plasticity in object representations in these medial temporal lobe structures (see Banks et al., 2014, for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of learning-related plasticity in MTL.

claim: The current findings highlight the critical value of probing the subjective appreciation of visual object similarities and their variability across observers for a complete understanding of the transformation of neural representations from posterior regions to those at the apex of the VVS.
source: Regardless of the outcome of such future research, the current findings highlight the critical value of probing the subjective appreciation of visual object similarities, and their variability across observers, for a complete understanding of the transformation of neural representations from posterior regions to those at the apex of the VVS.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: All participants were right handed, fluent in English, and had no known history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
source: All participants were right handed, fluent in English, and had no known history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Stimuli were selected with varying normative levels of perceived visual similarity from the Migo Normative Database.
source: In order to investigate object representations at the exemplar level, we selected stimuli with varying normative levels of perceived visual similarity from the Migo Normative Database (Migo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about stimulus selection with citation.

claim: Only stimuli with perceived similarity ratings similar to those from the normative database were selected based on findings from a pilot study.
source: Based on findings from a pilot study (n = 40), only stimuli with perceived similarity ratings similar to those from the normative database were selected.
evidence: This is a direct statement about stimulus validation.

claim: Participants were instructed to use the entire space within the circle and make sure they compared each stimulus to every other stimulus during the iMDS task.
source: They were instructed to use the entire space within the circle, and make sure they compared each stimulus to every other stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct statement about task instructions.

claim: A MATLAB-based toolbox was used to calculate distances between each pair of exemplars and convert these distances to dissimilarity percentiles.
source: A MATLAB-based toolbox was used to calculate distances between each pair of exemplars, and to convert these distances to dissimilarity percentiles (Kriegeskorte and Mur, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data analysis methods with citation.

claim: Any values that did not allow for at least 0.1 dissimilarity percentile between successive levels were excluded to ensure non-overlapping levels of perceived similarity.
source: In order to ensure that the different levels of perceived similarity were nonoverlapping, any values that did not allow for at least 0.1 dissimilarity percentile between each of the successive levels (i.e., high-middle and middle-low) was excluded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data processing criteria.

claim: The range of dissimilarity percentiles did not differ significantly between the different levels of perceived similarity.
source: The range of dissimilarity percentiles did not differ significantly between the different levels of perceived similarity (p > 0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HMAX is designed as a four-layer hierarchical feed-forward structure similar to that previously described in the VVS.
source: In this way, HMAX is designed as a four-layer hierarchical feed-forward structure similar to that previously described in the VVS.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational model architecture based on prior work.

claim: The output layer of HMAX captures an object's shape over activation patterns and has been shown to correspond to activation patterns in IT cortex and LOC.
source: The output layer of HMAX captures an object's shape over activation patterns and has been shown to correspond to activation patterns in IT cortex and LOC (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on HMAX.

claim: Participants used their right index and middle finger to respond, with response assignment counterbalanced across participants.
source: Participants used their right index and middle finger to respond, with response assignment counterbalanced across participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Only the no-response trials were used in the fMRI analysis to avoid motor confounds associated with button presses.
source: Of the three trial types—same exemplar, same category, different category—only the no-response trials (i.e., different category) were used in the fMRI analysis to avoid motor confounds associated with button presses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis approach.

claim: None of the trials considered for assessment of similarity in activation patterns were immediate neighbours.
source: By extension, none of the trials considered for assessment of similarity in activation patterns were immediate neighbours.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design to avoid temporal confounds.

claim: Prior to scanning, each participant completed a 5-min practice task with images from categories not included in the functional scanning experiment.
source: Prior to scanning, each participant completed a 5-min practice task with images from categories not included in the functional scanning experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: A whole head MP-RAGE volume was acquired with TE = 2.28 ms, TR = 2400 ms, TI = 1060 ms, resolution = 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 mm isometric.
source: Before the fMRI session, a whole head MP-RAGE volume (TE = 2.28 ms, TR = 2400 ms, TI = 1060 ms, resolution = 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 mm isometric) was acquired.
evidence: This is a direct statement about MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Four fMRI runs were acquired, each with 300 volumes consisting of 42 T2*-weighted slices with a resolution of 1.7 × 1.7 mm.
source: This was followed by four fMRI runs, each with 300 volumes, which consisted of 42 T2*-weighted slices with a resolution of 1.7 × 1.7 mm (TE = 30 ms, TR = 1000 ms, slice thickness 1.7 mm, FOV 200 mm, parallel imaging with grappa factor 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: T2*-weighted slices were acquired in odd-even interleaved fashion in the anterior to posterior direction.
source: The T2* slices were acquired in odd-even interleaved fashion in the anterior to posterior direction.
evidence: This is a direct statement about MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Total duration of MRI acquisition was approximately 60 minutes.
source: Total duration of MRI acquisition was approximately 60 min.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scanning session duration.

claim: MRI data were converted to brain imaging data structure and ran through fmriprep-v1.1.8.
source: MRI data were converted to brain imaging data structure (Gorgolewski et al., 2016) and ran through fmriprep-v1.1.8 (Esteban et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement about preprocessing methods with citations.

claim: Preprocessing included motion correction, slice time correction, susceptibility distortion correction, registration from EPI to T1w image, and confounds estimated.
source: This preprocessing included motion correction, slice time correction, susceptibility distortion correction, registration from EPI to T1w image, and confounds estimated (e.g., tCompCor, aCompCor, and framewise displacement).
evidence: This is a direct statement about preprocessing steps.

claim: Component based noise correction was performed using anatomical and temporal CompCor by adding these confound estimates as regressors in SPM12 during a first-level GLM.
source: Component based noise correction was performed using anatomical and temporal CompCor, aCompCor, and tCompCor, by adding these confound estimates as regressors in SPM12 during a first-level general linear model (GLM) (Behzadi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement about preprocessing methods with citation.

claim: First-level analyses were conducted in native space for each participant with no spatial smoothing to preserve ultra-high-resolution patterns of activity for multivariate pattern analyses.
source: First-level analyses were conducted in native space for each participant with no spatial smoothing to preserve ultra-high-resolution patterns of activity for multivariate pattern analyses (MVPA).
evidence: This is a direct statement about analysis approach.

claim: Exemplar-specific multivoxel activity patterns were estimated in 40 separate general linear models using the mean activity of the no-response trials across runs.
source: Exemplar-specific multivoxel activity patterns were estimated in 40 separate general linear models using the mean activity of the no-response trials across runs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis approach.

claim: A probabilistic atlas was used to define EVC and TP.
source: A probabilistic atlas was used to define EVC (Wang et al., 2015) and TP (Fischl, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ROI definition methods with citations.

claim: A functional localizer was used to define LOC as the contiguous voxels located along the lateral extent of the occipital lobe that responded more strongly to intact objects than scrambled objects.
source: A functional localizer was used to define LOC as the contiguous voxels located along the lateral extent of the occipital lobe that responded more strongly to intact objects than scrambled objects (p < 0.01, uncorrected; Proklova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ROI definition methods with citation.

claim: Linear correlation distances (Pearson's r) were calculated between all pairs of exemplar-specific multivoxel patterns using CoSMoMVPA toolbox in Matlab.
source: For each ROI, linear correlation distances (Pearson's r) were calculated between all pairs of exemplar-specific multivoxel patterns using CoSMoMVPA toolbox in Matlab (Oosterhof et al., 2016) across all voxels.
evidence: This is a direct statement about analysis methods with citation.

claim: A 100-voxel neighbourhood was defined around each surface voxel for whole-volume searchlight RSA.
source: Specifically, we defined a 100-voxel neighbourhood around each surface voxel, and computed a brain-based RDM within this region, analogous to the ROI-based RSA.
evidence: This is a direct statement about searchlight analysis parameters.

claim: TFCE was used to correct for multiple comparisons with a cluster threshold of p < 0.05.
source: TFCE was used to correct for multiple comparisons with a cluster threshold of p < 0.05 (Smith and Nichols, 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical correction methods with citation.
